comparison: Perfect agreement on bladder weight and anatomical findings (C13-C15, C54-C57). Both evaluations support these claims with OpenEval noting statistical significance and peer reviewers accepting the anatomical evidence without critique.

Both support normalization of muscarinic receptor-mediated contractility (C84-C86). OpenEval interprets this as normalization while one peer reviewer appears to misinterpret the data as showing increased sensitivity, though both ultimately support the finding.

Both support therapeutic benefit in female detrusor contractility (C95-C98). OpenEval notes incomplete normalization compared to males, while peer reviewers acknowledge functional improvements with general concerns about variability.

Both support lack of kidney transduction (C73, C135). OpenEval provides detailed negative data with positive controls, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this biodistribution profile without raising concerns.

Both identify the lack of in vivo functional studies (C107) as a limitation. OpenEval rates this as SUPPORTED (appropriate acknowledgment), while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, explicitly requesting void spot assays or cystometry to strengthen the evidence.

Both support liver transduction findings (C49-C50, C68-C71). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative analysis and notes safety concerns, while peer reviewers confirm dose-dependent liver transduction without raising safety issues at this stage.

Both support urethral relaxation improvements (C74-C78). OpenEval emphasizes substantial functional improvement with appropriate statistics, while peer reviewers confirm the finding but note variability at lower frequencies.

Both support detrusor contractility improvements (C79-C83). OpenEval highlights statistical significance and KCl controls, while peer reviewers confirm functional restoration but note variability at lower frequencies across replicates.

Significant disagreement on bladder transduction findings (C65-C67). OpenEval supports the finding with acknowledgment of uncertainty about rare positive foci, while peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, calling the undetectable bladder HPSE2 'a big question' for functional correction.

Both rate mechanism uncertainty (C108-C110) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes limitations in distinguishing neurogenic from myogenic contributions, while peer reviewers question how functional correction occurs without detectable bladder HPSE2 expression.

Both support therapeutic efficacy in female mice (C89-C94). OpenEval provides detailed analysis noting greater magnitude of effect than males, while peer reviewers acknowledge functional restoration without separately critiquing female data.
Both support sex differences in disease phenotype (C99, C102). OpenEval documents sexual dimorphism in UFS pathophysiology, while peer reviewers acknowledge sex differences in carbachol response.

Both support persistence of growth impairment despite bladder correction (C52-C53, C112-C114). OpenEval emphasizes dissociation of phenotypes suggesting distinct mechanisms, while peer reviewers accept the finding without raising concerns.

Both rate the liver-mediated systemic effect hypothesis (C138) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes the speculation lacks direct evidence of circulating protein, while peer reviewers emphasize this relates to concerns about the discrepancy in HPSE2 expression between tissues.

Both support successful transduction and expression (C44-C48, C58-C61). OpenEval provides comprehensive evidence from multiple techniques showing dose-dependent efficiency, while peer reviewers explicitly confirm convincing demonstration of AAV9/HPSE2 expression in pelvic ganglia.

Both support safety findings (C42-C43). OpenEval notes adequate safety for proof-of-concept but incomplete toxicity evaluation, while peer reviewers state no impact on body weight or liver health suggesting the approach was safe.

Both support safety assessment (C51, C72). OpenEval acknowledges limitation that transient liver damage cannot be excluded without blood tests, while peer reviewers confirm safety over the evaluated timeframe.

Both support protein expression findings (C62-C64). OpenEval confirms functional expression through immunohistochemistry, while peer reviewers acknowledge corresponding increase in heparanase-2 protein in pelvic ganglia.

Both support proof-of-concept demonstration (C106). OpenEval integrates transduction efficiency with functional outcomes for therapeutic threshold implications, while peer reviewers emphasize this demonstrates feasibility of AAV9-based gene therapy for UFS.

Both support sex differences documentation (C101). OpenEval provides detailed comparison of myography data between sexes, while peer reviewers acknowledge sex differences in the mutant phenotype without raising concerns.
